content: Multiple-micronutrient (MMN) deficiencies are common among women of reproductive age in lowand middle-income countries, and these deficiencies are often worsened during pregnancy due to the increased nutritional demands of the developing fetus. This can lead to adverse outcomes for both the mother and the baby. There is ongoing debate about whether MMN supplementation should replace the standard practice of providing iron and folic acid supplements during pregnancy. Since the last update of this Cochrane Review in 2017, new evidence from several trials has emerged, which is critical for shaping policies on micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of oral MMN supplementation during pregnancy on maternal, fetal, and infant health outcomes. For the 2018 update, a comprehensive search was conducted on February 23, 2018, using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Experts in the field were also contacted to identify additional or ongoing trials. The review included all prospective randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the effects of MMN supplementation with iron and folic acid on pregnancy outcomes, regardless of language or publication status. Cluster-randomized trials were included, but quasi-randomized trials were excluded. Abstracts of trial reports were eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified accuracy. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 21 trials involving 142,496 women were deemed eligible for inclusion, but data were contributed by 20 trials involving 141,849 women. Of these, 19 trials were conducted in lowand middle-income countries and compared MMN supplementation with iron and folic acid to iron alone (with or without folic acid). One trial conducted in the UK compared MMN supplementation to a placebo. Eight of the trials were cluster-randomized. The findings showed that MMN supplementation likely resulted in a slight reduction in preterm births (risk ratio [RR] 0.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.90 to 1.01; moderate-quality evidence) and in the number of babies considered small-for-gestational-age (SGA) (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.97; moderate-quality evidence). However, the confidence interval for preterm births crossed the line of no effect. MMN supplementation significantly reduced the number of newborns with low birthweight (LBW) (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.91; high-quality evidence). No differences were observed between groups for perinatal mortality (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.11; high-quality evidence). MMN supplementation slightly reduced stillbirths (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.04; high-quality evidence), but the confidence interval again crossed the line of no effect. There was no significant impact on neonatal mortality (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.12; high-quality evidence). For other maternal and pregnancy outcomes, MMN supplementation showed little or no difference. These outcomes included maternal anemia in the third trimester (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.15), maternal mortality (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.54), miscarriage (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.04), cesarean delivery (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.29), and congenital anomalies (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.25 to 7.12). However, MMN supplementation likely reduced the incidence of very preterm births (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.93; moderate-quality evidence). Some clinically important outcomes could not be assessed due to insufficient or unavailable data. The overall quality of evidence for the primary outcomes was rated as moderate to high. High-quality evidence was available for outcomes such as LBW, perinatal mortality, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. Moderate-quality evidence was available for preterm birth and SGA, with these outcomes downgraded due to potential publication bias indicated by funnel plot asymmetry. Sensitivity analyses excluding trials with high levels of sample attrition (>20%) showed consistent results with the main analyses. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity, examining factors such as maternal height, body mass index (BMI), timing of supplementation, iron dose, and MMN formulation (UNIMMAP versus non-UNIMMAP). Greater reductions in preterm births were observed among women with low BMI and those who received non-UNIMMAP supplements. Subgroup differences were also noted for maternal BMI and height in relation to SGA, with greater impacts seen in women with higher BMI and height. For perinatal mortality, substantial statistical heterogeneity was observed, and subgroup analysis suggested that later initiation of supplementation had a higher impact. Findings from other subgroup analyses were inconclusive. A single trial conducted in the UK compared MMN supplementation to a placebo. This trial found no significant effects on preterm births, SGA, or LBW but did report a reduction in maternal anemia in the third trimester (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.85). Other outcomes were not measured in this trial. In conclusion, MMN supplementation during pregnancy, when combined with iron and folic acid, had a positive impact on several birth outcomes. It reduced the incidence of LBW and likely reduced the number of babies considered SGA and preterm births. However, no significant benefits or harms were observed for mortality outcomes, including stillbirths, perinatal mortality, and neonatal mortality. These findings may support the replacement of iron and folic acid supplements with MMN supplements for pregnant women in lowand middle-income countries.
